prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty, opening many-body-aware precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as my single-part configuration; round 1 has not changed it, but it has sharpened what I think the citation must say. The scientific core is that magic-wavelength trapping removes the lattice light shift, so that very many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without trap-induced perturbation. That is a separable conceptual step, distinct from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012), and it is what makes statistical power at the 1e-18 level possible. Ye's group then supplied the systematic control and the many-body-aware operation that turned the concept into the most accurate measurement in any field. Independent reproduction in Sr and Yb laboratories is as strong as for anything on this list. To the chair's question about delivered rather than prospective results: from my recollection, which I have not re-verified here, the clock comparisons already constrain variation of fundamental constants and the clocks have resolved gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale height differences within a single sample, and clock-based geodesy has been demonstrated in the field. These are results about nature obtained with the instrument, not only promises. I would not claim a dark-matter detection or a completed redefinition of the second. As an atomic theorist I add that the credibility of the accuracy claims rests on relativistic atomic structure, polarisability and blackbody-shift calculations that are well understood, which is part of why I trust the performance numbers.
statement.case_against: The category question is real and I do not dismiss it: a committee that wants the prize to reward a change in what physicists can think, rather than in what they can measure, would reasonably prefer B018. Credit is also narrower than the history. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, the PTB and NIST groups, the Yb and Hg communities and the ion-clock lineage all made decisive contributions that a two-name prize cannot name, so the citation has to claim the invention and the realisation, and nothing broader. Finally the redefinition of the second has not been decided, so part of the payoff remains prospective. I still judge these as qualifications and not disqualifications, because the invention is separable, the confirmation is overwhelming, and I see no rival configuration in this room that is cleaner on credit.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B009 from fifth to the preferred position but warns that broad support is not depth of scientific weight, that the clock is a metrology invention after 2005 and 2012, and that it has not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of its own; he also argues that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission prevents him from repairing B018 within three names.
responses.response: Your warning about mistaking breadth for depth is fair, and I have tried to test it rather than lean on the count. I would put the point differently from the way you do, though: the clocks have already produced measurements that bear on physics, namely constraints on drifts in fundamental constants from clock-ratio comparisons and the redshift measured over very small height differences, and I recall these from the literature rather than from this file. They are not a discovery of new physics, and I agree that none should be claimed. On B018 I agree that the BHZ and three-dimensional omissions cannot be repaired within three names, which is exactly why I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred configuration even though it is my second choice.

responses.point: Eriksson says he moved from B041 first and B009 fifth, that a clean experimental result against which theory can be tested matters more than the method-versus-discovery label, but that B009 would drop if the committee preferred a change in what physicists can think about over what they can measure.
responses.response: I agree that testability against theory is a strength here, and as a theorist I would say the clock is unusually well-posed for that: the systematic budget can be checked against calculated polarisabilities and shifts. I do not think the invention merely sharpens an existing measurement, however. Removing the light shift for trapped neutral atoms changed which experiments are possible, since it brought many-body effects such as collisional and lattice-induced shifts into the clock itself, and that is new physics inside the instrument. I take your conditional seriously, and if the committee does choose a field-opening criterion above all others, I would then prefer B018 over B041, which as you note has had no support except your own.

responses.point: Kroll replies that the proposal precedes the first demonstrations and the later accuracy milestones, so the sequence supports Katori for the concept and the strontium demonstration and Ye for the performance, that the Boulder connection to the Hall laboratory is a disclosed professional link and not a stake, and that distinctness from 2005 and 2012 is answered by citation wording.
responses.response: I agree on the priority sequence and on wording as the answer to the distinctness concern, and I have made the citation carry that: it names the invention and the realisation separately, and it does not claim the comb or ion control. On your disclosure, a research period in the Hall laboratory is a training connection that, in my view, requires recording and not recusal, since you do not share a project with Ye or Katori and no stake follows. I would let the committee note it in the minutes and proceed. Where I would hold the line is on your raising of waiting for the redefinition of the second: the award is for the invention and its demonstrated accuracy, which stand regardless of the metrological decision.

responses.point: Olsson says the magic-wavelength idea is separable and original, that the lack of a completed redefinition of the second is a pending-payoff criticism, and that a two-name prize simplifies the history of Lemonde, Gill, Hinkley, Ludlow and others; her secondary alternative B017 is a field-adjacent disclosure.
responses.response: I agree with your reading that separability and originality are what answer the pending-redefinition criticism, and I would add that the citation should not mention the redefinition at all. On credit, I think your list of other groups is right and I do not see a way to add them within three names without weakening the cleanest part of the case, so I would rather the citation say exactly what Katori and Ye did. I note that you list B017 only as a secondary alternative; I would not rank it against B009 on credit clarity, since the opening support, as the shortlist shows, rests on one first-place ranking and two ranked members in total.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the lattice clock as discovery-class or as precision instrumentation after 2005 and 2012; I judge the invention separable but cannot settle this for others.
My statements about delivered results (constants constraints, millimetre-scale redshift, clock-based geodesy) are from recollection and are not verified from the supplied record.
Whether a two-name citation can state clearly enough what it does not credit (other lattice-clock groups, ion clocks, combs).
If B018 were preferred, how the omissions of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the three-dimensional topological-insulator work would be handled within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B009 is apparent from my profile: Katori and Ye are not among my documented collaborators. I repeat the earlier disclosure of professional proximity: I am an atomic theorist with documented collaborations with the Lund attosecond group including Anne L'Huillier, with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and with Luca Argenti, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato, none of whom is a credited name on the shortlist. I note Kroll's disclosed Boulder connection and consider recording it sufficient. B009, B014 and B010 lie in my own broad field, so I still flag a disciplinary bias that I cannot fully correct for.
